findings.text: Four tracing flags encode guest execution context using bits zero through three. One indicates protected mode enable, one indicates virtual 8086 mode, and two capture code segment size attributes that together distinguish real mode from 16, 32 and 64 bit protected operation.

Decoding maps each abstract x86 emulation mode to a flag combination, clearing all flags for real mode and setting protected, virtual, or segment size bits for other modes, with unknown modes yielding all bits set. Tracing then renders each combination with a distinct short name for real, virtual 16, and protected 16, 32 and 64 bit states.
Host clock tracing supports two modes, an absent clock and a timestamp counter clock, each with a short display name for trace output.
Interrupt virtualization inhibit tracing emits the numeric mask and, only when nonzero, appends a separator plus a symbolic breakdown of the set reasons.
Trace generation resolves its companion definitions under the x86 virtualization directory using a fixed leaf name.

Two task state layouts cover wide and narrow guests. Both preserve privilege stacks, processor state, general registers and segment state with descriptor references, while the wide form uses larger fields and carries additional control and I O permission metadata.

I O permission base offset is 0x66 and base task state length is 0x68. Derived sizes are 8192 bytes for the permission bitmap and 32 bytes for redirection, with real mode total defined as base plus redirection plus bitmap plus one terminator byte.
Guest entry options occupy bits zero, one and two. They select resume behavior, preservation of speculation control state, and clearing of CPU buffers for entries that may follow device emulation.
Machine word length in bytes is derived by dividing the bits per long value by eight.
Processor trace virtualization uses zero for system wide operation and one for host guest operation.

Nested capability storage keeps true forms of processor, secondary, pin, exit and entry controls with miscellaneous data, plus paging and identifier capabilities and fixed control and enumeration values. Host configuration aggregates basic state, pin and processor controls including secondary and tertiary levels, exit and entry controls, miscellaneous data and the nested block. A compact pair separately caches paging and identifier features.

One group of capability queries reports host support for basic I O handling, error code behavior, virtual interrupts, preemption timing, posted delivery, loading or saving of extended and performance and protection state, shadowing, bitmap use, and activation of further control levels.

Another group reports secondary and tertiary execution controls for APIC virtualization, paging, counter and identifier handling, cache and guest mode behavior, register and delivery support, exiting on pause, random, identifier, function, enclave, seed, logging, state, wait, scaling and lock events, plus third level interrupt virtualization.

Composite queries combine base checks. Flexpriority needs shadowing with APIC access support, full APIC virtualization needs register plus delivery plus posted support, shadow control needs writability plus secondary enablement, one protection query is emulated when hardware lacks it but descriptor handling exists, one shadowing query adds an in kernel controller requirement, and trace support needs misc plus secondary plus entry enablement together.

Paging and identifier queries report walk depth, memory type, large page availability, dirty tracking and invalidation extents. A helper selects the largest advertised large page level, preferring gigabyte over megabyte pages and otherwise using small pages.

Trace mode checks compare global mode against system and host guest values, a sampling feature check requires hardware support with mediated use disabled and a capability flag set, and two checks report notification exiting and mode based execution control.

Exit reason combines a full word view with a field view holding a wide basic code and status flags for lock detection, enclave execution, management interrupts and entry failure, with other bits reserved. Per CPU virtualization state holds posted interrupt data with wakeup linkage, cached exit reason and qualification, flags for loaded guest state and required emulation, and a host base register on wide builds.
Trust domain detection has two build variants. One compares machine type against the trust domain type for machine and CPU handles, the other always reports false when the feature is not built.

Private address detection treats non direct addresses as private for trust domains. Violation handling translates qualification into fault semantics for write, fetch, present, user and guest translation stages, marks private access when relevant, and delegates to the common page fault path.

Posted delivery marks the vector pending and ensures a single outstanding notification before triggering. Triggering notifies a remote running guest via interprocessor interrupt and otherwise wakes the target for synchronization on next entry. Ordering between mode observation and notification state is required to avoid lost wakeups.

Nested pointer lookup yields an invalid handle when assist setup fails or enlightened entry is disabled, otherwise the current nested control address. Version lookup advertises support from first through current version when virtualization and enlightened use are enabled, otherwise zero.

Enlightened support defines revision and control categories with per revision allowed masks, excluding scaling from one category, plus lookup and a guest capability gate for performance fields. Filtering restricts control registers to allowed bits and further clears performance bits when the guest lacks the enabling flag.
A log helper prefixes messages with the module name and a shorthand names the nested entry consistency check used during validation.
Headers use include guards to prevent multiple inclusion.
